artwork.title: Sarcophagus of the Spouses

lessons.title: A couple on a clay couch

n1.text: A man and a woman, life-size, half-recline side by side on a couch. They are made of painted clay.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Look at his right hand resting on her shoulder. Then compare the colour of their skin.

q1.text: What are the two of them leaning on?

b1a.text: Not cloaks: cushions made to look like skins.

correction.tempting: His cloak is draped around him.
correction.truth: Each leans on a cushion shaped like a wineskin, an animal skin filled with air.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Report on the Campana Collection (1856); Campana's catalogue.

b1b.text: Yes. Each leans on a cushion shaped like a wineskin: an animal skin blown up with air.

b1c.text: Not stone: like the rest, the cushions are clay.

correction.tempting: The cushions look firm and solid.
correction.truth: They are clay cushions shaped like wineskins, animal skins filled with air.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Report on the Campana Collection (1856); Campana's catalogue.

n6.text: Couch, cushions, two people side by side: they half-recline the way diners did at a banquet.

q5.text: Would a real Etruscan wife recline beside her husband at a banquet?

choices.label: No: only men reclined to eat

b5a.text: Yes. Rome's Villa Giulia museum describes the Etruscan woman beside the man at the banquet. A Greek source agrees: Aristotle wrote that Etruscans dine reclining with their women, under one cover.

b5b.text: Not in Etruria: women reclined too.

correction.tempting: Reclining to dine can sound like a man's privilege.
correction.truth: Etruscan women reclined beside the men. Aristotle wrote that Etruscans dine reclining with their women, under one cover.
correction.evidence: Villa Giulia museum, Rome; Aristotle, quoted by Athenaeus (tr. Yonge, 1854).

b5c.text: Not only in death: it was a real custom.

correction.tempting: This couple lies on a tomb monument.
correction.truth: The tomb recalls a real custom: Etruscan women reclined beside the men at banquets.
correction.evidence: Villa Giulia museum, Rome; Aristotle, quoted by Athenaeus (tr. Yonge, 1854).

n2.text: Some paint survives. His skin is red and hers is pale. Beneath them, the couch forms a chest.

q2.text: Was the chest made for a body, or for ashes?

choices.label: Surely a coffin for a body

b2a.text: That is one view, not a settled fact.

correction.tempting: It is large and is called a sarcophagus.
correction.truth: The Louvre puts a question mark on both 'sarcophagus' and 'urn'; Rome's Villa Giulia calls its similar couple an urn.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Villa Giulia museum, Rome.

b2b.text: That is one view, not a settled fact.

correction.tempting: A similar monument in Rome is called an urn.
correction.truth: The Louvre puts a question mark on both words, and the 1850s catalogue called it a sarcophagus.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Campana's catalogue; Report on the Campana Collection (1856).

b2c.text: Yes. The Louvre records it as 'sarcophagus (?)' and 'urn (?)'. Others have called similar chests coffins, or urns for ashes.

n3.text: It came out of the ground at Cerveteri, ancient Caere, in 1845–46, the winter the Marquis Giampietro Campana was digging there.

q3.text: How did it reach the Louvre?

b3a.text: Yes. Campana was tried for embezzlement in 1857 and his collection was seized and sold. Napoleon III bought most of it, and the Louvre records this work as bought in 1861.

b3b.text: No gift: Campana lost his collection.

correction.tempting: It was in Campana's collection in Rome.
correction.truth: After his trial in 1857, his collection was sold, and Napoleon III bought most of it.
correction.evidence: The Louvre; Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani).

b3c.text: No French dig: it was found in Italy.

correction.tempting: It is now in a French museum.
correction.truth: It was found at Cerveteri and came to the Louvre with the Campana collection, bought in 1861.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani).

n7.text: Campana's collection was enormous: the Louvre calls it the most ambitious private collection of the 19th century.

q6.text: Who bought major works from Campana's collection before Napoleon III?

choices.label: No one: Napoleon III bought it all

b6a.text: Not the pope: the Papal State sold the collection.

correction.tempting: The Papal State seized Campana's collection.
correction.truth: The Papal State sold it. In 1861 Tsar Alexander II bought major works, which went to the Hermitage.
correction.evidence: The Louvre; Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani).

b6b.text: Not all of it: a tsar bought first.

correction.tempting: Napoleon III bought the bulk of it.
correction.truth: Before his purchase, Tsar Alexander II bought major works in 1861 for the Hermitage.
correction.evidence: The Louvre; Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani).

b6c.text: Yes. In 1861 Tsar Alexander II bought major works for the Hermitage, almost six hundred pieces according to Italy's Dizionario Biografico. Napoleon III then bought the rest.

n4.text: Some details are lost. The man's left hand is gone, and so are things the couple once held.

q4.text: What were the holes in their hands for?

choices.label: Fixing the lid to the chest
Letting air out in the kiln

b4a.text: No: the holes are in the hands, not the edges.

correction.tempting: The lid had to sit firmly on the chest.
correction.truth: Holes in the hands held objects or ornaments of another material, now lost.
correction.evidence: Report on the Campana Collection (1856); Campana's catalogue.

b4b.text: Yes. The holes held objects or ornaments of another material, now lost. What they were is unknown.

b4c.text: They held things: objects of another material.

correction.tempting: They are small, neat round holes.
correction.truth: The 1850s writers saw the holes as fixings for objects or ornaments, now lost.
correction.evidence: Report on the Campana Collection (1856); Campana's catalogue.

n5.text: Two figures in painted clay, still side by side. They lie in Room 663, the Salle des Séances, on Floor 1 of the Sully wing.

lessons.takeaway: An Etruscan couple in painted clay from Cerveteri, reclining as at a banquet, as Etruscan wives really did: whether the chest held a body or ashes is still debated, and after a tsar took his pick, Napoleon III's purchase of the Campana collection brought it to Paris.
